chapter_text:
CHAPTER 8 - KINETIC THEORY OF GASES

Introduction

Gases are the simplest state of matter to model. Their molecules are far apart, move almost freely, and interact only during brief collisions. This simplicity lets us build a complete quantitative theory - the KINETIC THEORY OF GASES - that connects the invisible microscopic motion of molecules to the measurable macroscopic properties of a gas such as pressure, temperature and internal energy. In this chapter we first recall the experimental gas laws and the ideal gas equation, then set out the postulates of kinetic theory, derive the pressure of an ideal gas, interpret temperature as molecular kinetic energy, define molecular speeds, and finally apply the law of equipartition of energy to obtain the specific heats of gases. We close with the ideas of mean free path and the Maxwell speed distribution.

8.1 THE GAS LAWS AND THE IDEAL GAS EQUATION

Three experimental laws, discovered before any molecular picture existed, describe how the pressure P, volume V and absolute (Kelvin) temperature T of a fixed mass of gas are related.

Boyle's law (1662): at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume. P is proportional to 1/V, so PV = constant. On a P-V graph the isotherm is a rectangular hyperbola.

Charles' law (1787): at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. V is proportional to T, so V/T = constant.

Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law: at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. P/T = constant.

Combining the three gives the combined gas law PV/T = constant. Bringing in Avogadro's law - equal volumes of all gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules - fixes the constant to be proportional to the amount of gas, and we arrive at the IDEAL GAS EQUATION:

   PV = n R T

Here n is the number of moles, and R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1 is the universal gas constant. If N is the actual number of molecules and N_A = 6.022 x 10^23 per mole is Avogadro's number, then n = N/N_A and we may write

   PV = N k_B T,   where k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1

is BOLTZMANN'S CONSTANT. A gas that obeys PV = nRT exactly at all pressures and temperatures is called an IDEAL gas. Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature, where the molecules are far apart and intermolecular forces are negligible.

8.2 POSTULATES OF THE KINETIC THEORY

The kinetic theory explains the gas laws by treating a gas as a very large number of tiny molecules in ceaseless random motion. Its main postulates are:
 1. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules moving randomly in all directions with all possible speeds.
 2. The size of a molecule is negligible compared with the average distance between molecules; the molecules themselves occupy negligible volume compared with the container.
 3. Molecules exert no force on one another except during collisions; between collisions they move in straight lines with constant velocity (Newton's first law).
 4. Collisions between molecules, and between a molecule and the walls, are perfectly ELASTIC - kinetic energy and momentum are conserved and no energy is lost.
 5. The duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions.
 6. The molecules obey Newton's laws of motion. Because the motion is random, at any instant as many molecules move in one direction as in the opposite direction, and all directions are equivalent.

8.3 PRESSURE OF AN IDEAL GAS

Pressure arises because molecules continually strike the walls of the container and rebound, each impact delivering a small impulse. Consider N molecules, each of mass m, in a cubical box of side L (volume V = L^3). Take one molecule with velocity components (v_x, v_y, v_z). When it strikes the wall perpendicular to the x-axis, the elastic collision reverses v_x, so the change in the molecule's momentum is -2 m v_x and the momentum given to the wall is 2 m v_x. The molecule travels a distance 2L between successive impacts on the same wall, taking a time 2L/v_x, so it strikes that wall v_x/(2L) times per second. The force this one molecule exerts on the wall is rate of change of momentum = (2 m v_x) x (v_x / 2L) = m v_x^2 / L.

Summing over all N molecules, the total force is (m/L)(v_x1^2 + v_x2^2 + ... ) = (m N / L) <v_x^2>, where <v_x^2> is the mean of the squared x-components. Pressure is force per unit area (area = L^2):

   P = (m N / L^3) <v_x^2> = (m N / V) <v_x^2>.

Because the motion is random, <v_x^2> = <v_y^2> = <v_z^2>, and since v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2 we have <v^2> = 3 <v_x^2>, i.e. <v_x^2> = <v^2>/3. Writing c_rms^2 = <v^2> for the mean-square speed,

   P = (1/3)(m N / V) c_rms^2.

Since the total mass is M = N m and the density is rho = M/V = N m / V, this is also

   P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.

This is the central result of kinetic theory: pressure equals one-third of the gas density times the mean-square molecular speed. The quantity c_rms = sqrt(<v^2>) is the ROOT-MEAN-SQUARE speed.

8.4 KINETIC INTERPRETATION OF TEMPERATURE

Rewrite the pressure result as P V = (1/3) N m c_rms^2. Multiply and divide the right side by 2:

   P V = (2/3) N x (1/2 m c_rms^2) = (2/3) N (KE_avg),

where KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 is the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule. But the ideal gas equation says P V = N k_B T. Comparing the two,

   (2/3) N (KE_avg) = N k_B T,   so   KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 = (3/2) k_B T.

This is the KINETIC INTERPRETATION OF TEMPERATURE: the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is directly proportional to the absolute temperature and is (3/2) k_B T. Temperature is a measure of the average molecular kinetic energy - it does not depend on the mass or the type of gas. At absolute zero (T = 0) molecular translational motion would cease. Because KE_avg is the same for all gases at a given T, a lighter molecule must move faster than a heavier one.

8.5 MOLECULAR SPEEDS

From KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T = (1/2) m c_rms^2 we solve for the rms speed:

   c_rms = sqrt(3 k_B T / m) = sqrt(3 R T / M),

where M = N_A m is the molar mass. The rms speed increases as the square root of temperature and decreases as the square root of molar mass. Real molecules have a spread of speeds described by the MAXWELL SPEED DISTRIBUTION - a curve that rises from zero, peaks, and tails off at high speed. Three characteristic speeds are defined:
 - Most probable speed c_mp = sqrt(2 R T / M) - the speed at the peak of the distribution.
 - Average (mean) speed c_avg = sqrt(8 R T / (pi M)).
 - Root-mean-square speed c_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M).
Their ratio is fixed: c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732. Thus c_rms is the largest and c_mp the smallest of the three, with c_avg between them (c_avg is about 0.92 c_rms).

8.6 DEGREES OF FREEDOM

A DEGREE OF FREEDOM is an independent way in which a molecule can store energy - an independent coordinate needed to describe its motion. A single atom (monatomic gas such as He, Ne, Ar) can only translate in the x, y and z directions, so it has 3 (translational) degrees of freedom. A diatomic molecule (such as O2, N2, H2) also rotates about two axes perpendicular to the bond, adding 2 rotational degrees of freedom, giving 5 at ordinary temperatures (vibration is frozen out and ignored at moderate temperatures). A non-linear polyatomic molecule has 3 translational + 3 rotational = 6 degrees of freedom.

8.7 LAW OF EQUIPARTITION OF ENERGY

The law of equipartition of energy states that, in thermal equilibrium at temperature T, the total energy of a molecule is shared EQUALLY among all its degrees of freedom, each degree of freedom carrying an average energy of (1/2) k_B T per molecule (or (1/2) R T per mole). This follows because the average translational KE (3/2) k_B T is shared equally among the three translational degrees of freedom, giving (1/2) k_B T each; the law extends the same share to rotational (and vibrational) degrees of freedom. A molecule with f degrees of freedom therefore has average energy (f/2) k_B T.

8.8 SPECIFIC HEATS OF GASES

The internal energy of one mole of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom is U = (f/2) R T. The molar specific heat at constant volume is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one mole by 1 K with the volume fixed:

   C_v = dU/dT = (f/2) R.

At constant pressure the gas also does work as it expands. For one mole, using PV = RT, the extra work per kelvin is R, so the molar specific heat at constant pressure is larger by R:

   C_p = C_v + R      (Mayer's relation),   i.e.   C_p - C_v = R.

The ratio of the two specific heats, gamma = C_p / C_v, is a useful fingerprint of molecular structure:
 - Monatomic gas: f = 3, C_v = (3/2)R, C_p = (5/2)R, gamma = 5/3 = 1.67.
 - Diatomic gas: f = 5, C_v = (5/2)R, C_p = (7/2)R, gamma = 7/5 = 1.40.
 - Non-linear polyatomic gas: f = 6, C_v = 3R, C_p = 4R, gamma = 4/3 = 1.33.
Because gamma decreases as the number of degrees of freedom increases, measuring gamma reveals whether a gas is monatomic, diatomic or polyatomic.

8.9 MEAN FREE PATH

Although molecules move at hundreds of metres per second, a given molecule travels only a very short distance before colliding with another. The MEAN FREE PATH (lambda) is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. It is given by

   lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n),

where d is the molecular diameter and n = N/V is the number of molecules per unit volume. The mean free path is larger when the gas is less dense (smaller n) and when the molecules are smaller (smaller d). At ordinary atmospheric pressure lambda is of the order of 10^-7 m, roughly a hundred times the molecular diameter. This is why gases diffuse relatively slowly despite the high molecular speeds - molecules follow a long, zig-zag path.

8.10 WORKED EXAMPLES

Example 1. Find the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K (molar mass M = 32 x 10^-3 kg/mol). c_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M) = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300 / 0.032) = sqrt(233 800) = 484 m/s (approx).

Example 2. Find the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule at 300 K. KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300 = 6.21 x 10^-21 J. This value is the same for every ideal gas at 300 K, whatever the mass of its molecules.

Example 3. For a diatomic gas, C_v = (5/2)R = 20.8 J/mol/K, C_p = (7/2)R = 29.1 J/mol/K and gamma = 7/5 = 1.40. Note C_p - C_v = R = 8.31 J/mol/K.

Example 4. How many moles are contained in 0.0224 m^3 of an ideal gas at 273 K and 1.013 x 10^5 Pa? n = PV/RT = (1.013 x 10^5 x 0.0224)/(8.314 x 273) = 1.0 mol (this is the familiar molar volume of 22.4 litres at standard temperature and pressure).

SUMMARY

 - The experimental gas laws (Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac) combine with Avogadro's law into the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k_B T, with R = 8.314 J/mol/K and k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.
 - Kinetic theory models a gas as many tiny molecules in random motion with elastic collisions and negligible size and intermolecular force.
 - The pressure of an ideal gas is P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2 = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
 - Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy: KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 = (3/2) k_B T, independent of the gas.
 - c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M); the three characteristic speeds obey c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73.
 - Each degree of freedom carries average energy (1/2) k_B T (equipartition). Monatomic gases have 3 degrees of freedom, diatomic 5, non-linear polyatomic 6.
 - Specific heats: C_v = (f/2)R, C_p = C_v + R, gamma = C_p/C_v; gamma = 5/3 (monatomic), 7/5 (diatomic), 4/3 (polyatomic).
 - Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n) is the average distance between collisions, about 10^-7 m at atmospheric pressure.

sections.heading: Gas laws and the ideal gas equation
bullets: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, PV = constant for a fixed mass of gas (P inversely proportional to V).
Charles' law: at constant pressure, V/T = constant; Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, P/T = constant.
Combining these with Avogadro's law gives the ideal gas equation PV = nRT, where R = 8.314 J/mol/K.
Using n = N/N_A gives PV = N k_B T, where k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K is Boltzmann's constant.

sections.heading: Postulates of the kinetic theory
bullets: A gas is a very large number of identical molecules in ceaseless random motion in all directions.
Molecular size and volume are negligible compared with the average separation and the container volume.
Molecules exert no force on each other except during brief, perfectly elastic collisions; between collisions they move in straight lines.
The molecules obey Newton's laws; all directions of motion are equally likely.

sections.heading: Pressure of an ideal gas
bullets: Pressure comes from molecules striking the walls and reversing their momentum; each impact gives the wall an impulse 2 m v_x.
Summing over all molecules and using <v_x^2> = <v^2>/3 gives P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2.
In terms of density rho = Nm/V, this is P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
c_rms = sqrt(<v^2>) is the root-mean-square speed of the molecules.

sections.heading: Temperature and molecular speeds
bullets: Comparing P V = (2/3) N (KE_avg) with PV = N k_B T gives KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 = (3/2) k_B T.
Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy and is the same for all gases at a given T.
c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M); lighter molecules move faster than heavier ones at the same temperature.
The three characteristic speeds obey c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73.

Molar specific heats: C_v = (f/2)R and C_p = C_v + R, so C_p - C_v = R (Mayer's relation).
gamma = C_p/C_v is 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic and 4/3 for polyatomic gases. Mean free path lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n).

glossary.definition: A gas that obeys PV = nRT exactly; molecules have negligible size and no intermolecular forces except during collisions. Real gases approach this at low pressure and high temperature.
The relation PV = nRT = N k_B T linking pressure P, volume V, absolute temperature T and amount of gas.
The constant in PV = nRT, equal to 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1; the same for all gases.
The gas constant per molecule, k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1; appears in PV = N k_B T and KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T.
The number of molecules in one mole, 6.022 x 10^23 per mole.
The square root of the mean of the squared molecular speeds; c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3 k_B T / m).
The speed at the peak of the Maxwell distribution; c_mp = sqrt(2RT/M), the smallest of the three characteristic speeds.
The arithmetic mean of the molecular speeds; c_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), lying between c_mp and c_rms.
The result KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T: absolute temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule.
An independent way a molecule can store energy or an independent coordinate of its motion: 3 for monatomic, 5 for diatomic, 6 for non-linear polyatomic molecules.
In thermal equilibrium the energy is shared equally among all degrees of freedom, each carrying average energy (1/2) k_B T per molecule.

gamma = C_p/C_v; equals 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic and 4/3 for polyatomic gases.
The average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions; lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), about 10^-7 m at atmospheric pressure.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Kinetic Theory of Gases
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use R = 8.314 J/mol/K, k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K and N_A = 6.022 x 10^23 /mol where required. Show your working for numerical problems.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the pressure exerted by an ideal gas on the walls of its container, and hence show that P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
questions.answer: Consider N molecules each of mass m in a cube of side L (volume V = L^3). Take a molecule with x-velocity v_x hitting the wall perpendicular to the x-axis. The elastic collision reverses v_x, so momentum given to the wall per impact = 2 m v_x. The molecule returns to the same wall after travelling 2L, i.e. after time 2L/v_x, so it hits v_x/(2L) times per second. Force by this molecule = 2 m v_x x v_x/(2L) = m v_x^2 / L. Summing over all molecules, total force = (mN/L) <v_x^2>. Pressure = force / area = (mN/L)<v_x^2> / L^2 = (mN/V) <v_x^2>. Random motion gives <v_x^2> = <v_y^2> = <v_z^2> = <v^2>/3. Writing c_rms^2 = <v^2>: P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2. Since density rho = Nm/V, P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
questions.explanation: Full kinetic-theory derivation of gas pressure.

questions.question: State the postulates of the kinetic theory of gases.
questions.answer: (1) A gas has a very large number of identical molecules in random motion in all directions with all speeds. (2) The molecular size and volume are negligible compared with the intermolecular distance and container volume. (3) Molecules exert no force on each other except during collisions; between collisions they move in straight lines. (4) All collisions (molecule-molecule and molecule-wall) are perfectly elastic - kinetic energy and momentum are conserved. (5) The collision time is negligible compared with the time between collisions. (6) Molecules obey Newton's laws; all directions of motion are equally likely.

questions.question: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K. (Molar mass of O2 = 32 x 10^-3 kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300 / 0.032) = sqrt(7482.6/0.032) = sqrt(233 831) = 484 m/s (approximately). So oxygen molecules at 300 K have an rms speed of about 484 m/s.

questions.question: Find the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K. Is the value different for hydrogen and oxygen? (k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.)
questions.answer: KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300 = 6.21 x 10^-21 J. This value depends only on temperature, not on the type or mass of the gas, so it is the SAME for hydrogen and oxygen at 300 K. (Hydrogen molecules simply move faster because they are lighter.)
questions.explanation: KE_avg = (3/2)k_B T, independent of gas type.

questions.question: For a diatomic gas, calculate C_v, C_p and gamma. (R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: A diatomic molecule has f = 5 degrees of freedom (3 translational + 2 rotational). C_v = (f/2)R = (5/2)(8.314) = 20.8 J/mol/K. C_p = C_v + R = 20.8 + 8.314 = 29.1 J/mol/K. gamma = C_p/C_v = 29.1/20.8 = 7/5 = 1.40.

questions.question: Using the ideal gas equation, find the number of moles in 0.0224 m^3 of gas at 273 K and pressure 1.013 x 10^5 Pa.
questions.answer: n = PV/RT = (1.013 x 10^5 x 0.0224)/(8.314 x 273) = 2269.1 / 2269.7 = 1.0 mol (approximately). This is the standard result that one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP.

questions.question: State the law of equipartition of energy and use it to write the internal energy of one mole of a monatomic and of a diatomic ideal gas.
questions.answer: Law of equipartition: in thermal equilibrium the energy is shared equally among all degrees of freedom, each carrying average energy (1/2) k_B T per molecule, or (1/2) R T per mole. Internal energy of one mole with f degrees of freedom is U = (f/2) R T. Monatomic (f = 3): U = (3/2) R T. Diatomic (f = 5): U = (5/2) R T.

questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles' law, and write the combined ideal gas equation.
questions.answer: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume, so PV = constant. Charles' law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, so V/T = constant. Combining these with Gay-Lussac's law and Avogadro's law gives the ideal gas equation PV = nRT = N k_B T.

questions.question: What is meant by the mean free path of a gas molecule? Write its formula and state two factors that affect it.
questions.answer: The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. It is lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), where d is the molecular diameter and n = N/V is the number density. It increases when the gas is less dense (smaller n, e.g. lower pressure) and when the molecules are smaller (smaller d).

questions.question: The rms speed of a gas is 500 m/s at 300 K. What will it be at 1200 K?
questions.answer: c_rms is proportional to sqrt(T). Raising T from 300 K to 1200 K multiplies T by 4, so c_rms multiplies by sqrt(4) = 2. New c_rms = 2 x 500 = 1000 m/s.

questions.explanation: c_rms is the largest; c_mp is smallest.

questions.question: A monatomic gas molecule has 3 degrees of freedom.
For an ideal gas, C_p is greater than C_v.
The mean free path of a gas increases as its density decreases.
The equation PV = nRT is called the ____ equation.
The value of the universal gas constant R is ____ J/mol/K.
Boltzmann's constant k_B equals R divided by ____.
In kinetic theory, collisions between molecules are perfectly ____.
The pressure of an ideal gas is P = (1/3) ____ c_rms^2.
In the pressure derivation, the momentum given to the wall per molecular impact is ____.
The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2) ____ T.
Absolute temperature is a measure of the average ____ energy of gas molecules.
The rms speed is given by c_rms = sqrt(3RT/____).
The rms speed of a gas is directly proportional to the square root of its absolute ____.
A diatomic molecule at ordinary temperature has ____ degrees of freedom.
By the law of equipartition, each degree of freedom carries an average energy of ____ per molecule.
Mayer's relation states that C_p - C_v = ____.
For a monatomic gas the ratio gamma = C_p/C_v equals ____.
The average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions is called the ____.
State Boyle's law and Gay-Lussac's law.
questions.answer: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume (PV = constant). Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (P/T = constant).
questions.explanation: Two of the three gas laws.

questions.question: A gas occupies 2.0 litres at 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. If the temperature is kept constant and the pressure raised to 4.0 x 10^5 Pa, what is the new volume?
questions.answer: At constant temperature Boyle's law applies: P1 V1 = P2 V2. So V2 = P1 V1 / P2 = (1.0 x 10^5 x 2.0)/(4.0 x 10^5) = 0.5 litre.

questions.question: Distinguish between the universal gas constant R and Boltzmann's constant k_B.
questions.answer: R is the gas constant per MOLE, R = 8.314 J/mol/K, appearing in PV = nRT. k_B is the gas constant per MOLECULE, k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K, appearing in PV = N k_B T and KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T. They are related by R = k_B x N_A.

questions.question: List any three postulates of the kinetic theory of gases.
questions.answer: (1) A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in random motion in all directions. (2) The molecular size and volume are negligible compared with the intermolecular distance and container volume. (3) Molecules exert no force on one another except during perfectly elastic collisions; between collisions they move in straight lines at constant velocity.

questions.question: Why is the assumption of perfectly elastic collisions important in kinetic theory?
questions.answer: If collisions were not perfectly elastic, molecules would lose kinetic energy at each collision. The gas would gradually cool and the molecular motion would die away, contradicting the observation that a gas kept at constant temperature maintains constant pressure indefinitely. Perfectly elastic collisions conserve total kinetic energy, keeping the average molecular energy (and hence temperature and pressure) steady.

questions.question: Explain why the ideal gas model breaks down at very high pressure and very low temperature.
questions.answer: At high pressure the molecules are pushed close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume (postulate 2 fails). At low temperature the molecules move slowly and spend more time near each other, so intermolecular attractive forces become significant (postulate 3 fails). Under these conditions PV = nRT no longer holds accurately, and a real-gas equation (such as van der Waals') is needed.
questions.explanation: Two postulates fail at high P, low T.

questions.question: Starting from P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2, show that P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
questions.answer: The total mass of gas is M_total = N m (N molecules each of mass m). The density is rho = M_total/V = N m / V. Substituting N m / V = rho into P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2 gives P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.

questions.question: The density of a gas is 1.2 kg/m^3 and its pressure is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. Find the rms speed of its molecules.
questions.answer: From P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2, c_rms = sqrt(3P/rho) = sqrt(3 x 1.0 x 10^5 / 1.2) = sqrt(2.5 x 10^5) = 500 m/s (approximately).

questions.question: In the derivation of gas pressure, explain why <v_x^2> is replaced by <v^2>/3.
questions.answer: For any molecule v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2, so averaging over all molecules <v^2> = <v_x^2> + <v_y^2> + <v_z^2>. Because the molecular motion is completely random, no direction is preferred, so the three mean-square components are equal: <v_x^2> = <v_y^2> = <v_z^2>. Therefore <v^2> = 3<v_x^2>, giving <v_x^2> = <v^2>/3. This substitution converts the one-dimensional result into the full three-dimensional pressure.
questions.explanation: Isotropy makes the three components equal.

questions.question: Write the relation between the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule and temperature, and state what it tells us about temperature.
questions.answer: KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 = (3/2) k_B T. It tells us that the absolute temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules - the higher the temperature, the greater the average molecular kinetic energy.

questions.question: Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule at 27 C. (k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.)
Two vessels contain hydrogen and oxygen at the same temperature. Compare the average kinetic energies and the rms speeds of their molecules.
questions.answer: The average translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so it is the SAME for hydrogen and oxygen. However c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), so the lighter hydrogen (M = 2) has a much higher rms speed than the heavier oxygen (M = 32): the ratio is sqrt(32/2) = 4, so hydrogen molecules move four times faster.

questions.question: Write the formulae for the rms, average and most probable speeds and state their ratio.
questions.answer: c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M); c_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)); c_mp = sqrt(2RT/M). Their ratio is c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73.
questions.explanation: Three speeds and their fixed ratio.

questions.question: The rms speed of nitrogen molecules at 300 K is 517 m/s. Estimate the rms speed at 1200 K.
questions.answer: c_rms is proportional to sqrt(T). Going from 300 K to 1200 K multiplies T by 4, so c_rms multiplies by sqrt(4) = 2. New c_rms = 2 x 517 = 1034 m/s.

questions.question: Find the rms speed of hydrogen molecules at 300 K. (M = 2 x 10^-3 kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300 / 0.002) = sqrt(7482.6 / 0.002) = sqrt(3 741 300) = 1934 m/s (approximately). Hydrogen molecules are very fast because their molar mass is small.

questions.question: The rms speed of oxygen molecules is 484 m/s at 300 K. Find their average speed and most probable speed at the same temperature.
questions.answer: c_avg = c_rms x sqrt(8/(3 pi)) = 484 x 0.921 = 446 m/s. c_mp = c_rms x sqrt(2/3) = 484 x 0.816 = 395 m/s. (Using the fixed ratio c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73.)
questions.explanation: Scale c_rms by the fixed ratios.

questions.question: State the number of degrees of freedom of monatomic, diatomic and non-linear polyatomic gas molecules.
questions.answer: Monatomic: 3 (all translational). Diatomic (at ordinary temperature): 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Non-linear polyatomic: 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational). Vibrational degrees of freedom are ignored at moderate temperatures.
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom by molecular type.

questions.question: State the law of equipartition of energy and use it to obtain the internal energy of one mole of a diatomic gas.
questions.answer: Law of equipartition: in thermal equilibrium the total energy of a molecule is shared equally among all its degrees of freedom, each carrying average energy (1/2) k_B T per molecule (or (1/2) R T per mole). A diatomic molecule has 5 degrees of freedom, so the internal energy of one mole is U = 5 x (1/2) R T = (5/2) R T.

questions.question: Find the internal energy of 2 moles of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K. (R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: For a monatomic gas U per mole = (3/2) R T. For 2 moles U = 2 x (3/2) R T = 3 R T = 3 x 8.314 x 300 = 7483 J (about 7.48 kJ).

questions.question: State Mayer's relation and define the ratio of specific heats gamma.
questions.answer: Mayer's relation: for one mole of an ideal gas, C_p - C_v = R, where C_p and C_v are the molar specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume. The ratio of specific heats is gamma = C_p / C_v.

questions.question: For a monatomic gas, calculate C_v, C_p and gamma. (R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: Monatomic gas has f = 3 degrees of freedom. C_v = (3/2) R = 12.5 J/mol/K. C_p = C_v + R = 12.5 + 8.31 = 20.8 J/mol/K. gamma = C_p/C_v = 20.8/12.5 = 5/3 = 1.67.

questions.question: Define mean free path, give its formula, and explain why gases diffuse slowly even though molecules move very fast.
questions.answer: The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions: lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), where d is the molecular diameter and n the number density. Although molecular speeds are several hundred metres per second, each molecule collides very frequently (mean free path only about 10^-7 m at atmospheric pressure) and is deflected in a random direction at each collision. The resulting long zig-zag path means the net displacement grows slowly, so diffusion is slow.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the pressure of an ideal gas from the kinetic theory and hence obtain P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.
questions.answer: Take N molecules, each of mass m, in a cube of side L (volume V = L^3). Consider one molecule with velocity components (v_x, v_y, v_z). At the wall perpendicular to the x-axis, the elastic collision reverses v_x, so the momentum handed to the wall per impact is 2 m v_x. The molecule travels 2L before hitting the same wall again, so the time between impacts on that wall is 2L/v_x and it makes v_x/(2L) impacts per second. Force from this molecule = momentum per impact x impacts per second = 2 m v_x x v_x/(2L) = m v_x^2 / L. Summing over all molecules, total force = (m/L)(sum of v_x^2) = (mN/L) <v_x^2>, where <v_x^2> is the mean square x-velocity. Pressure = force/area = (mN/L)<v_x^2> / L^2 = (mN/V) <v_x^2>. Since motion is random, <v_x^2> = <v_y^2> = <v_z^2> = <v^2>/3. Writing c_rms^2 = <v^2>, P = (1/3)(mN/V) c_rms^2. With density rho = mN/V, this becomes P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.

questions.question: Starting from the kinetic pressure equation, show that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2) k_B T and explain the kinetic interpretation of temperature.
questions.answer: The kinetic result is PV = (1/3) N m c_rms^2. Multiply and divide the right side by 2: PV = (2/3) N x (1/2 m c_rms^2) = (2/3) N (KE_avg), where KE_avg = (1/2) m c_rms^2 is the average translational kinetic energy per molecule. The ideal gas law gives PV = N k_B T. Equating the two expressions: (2/3) N (KE_avg) = N k_B T, so KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T. This is the kinetic interpretation of temperature: the absolute temperature of a gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules. Because KE_avg depends only on T (not on the mass or type of molecule), all ideal gases at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy; lighter molecules simply move faster. At T = 0, KE_avg = 0, so molecular translational motion would cease.

questions.question: State the three experimental gas laws and show how they combine to give the ideal gas equation. Illustrate with the calculation of the volume of one mole of gas at STP.
questions.answer: Boyle's law (constant T): PV = constant. Charles' law (constant P): V/T = constant. Gay-Lussac's law (constant V): P/T = constant. Together these show that for a fixed mass of gas PV/T = constant. Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules, so the constant is proportional to the amount of gas (n moles): PV/T = nR, giving the ideal gas equation PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/mol/K. Using n = N/N_A gives the molecular form PV = N k_B T. Illustration: at STP (T = 273 K, P = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa) one mole (n = 1) occupies V = nRT/P = (1 x 8.314 x 273)/(1.013 x 10^5) = 0.0224 m^3 = 22.4 litres, the familiar molar volume.
questions.explanation: Gas laws -> ideal gas equation with STP example.

questions.question: Define the rms, average and most probable speeds of gas molecules. State their formulae and ratio, and calculate the three speeds for oxygen at 300 K. (M = 32 x 10^-3 kg/mol.)
questions.answer: The rms speed is the square root of the mean of the squared speeds; the average speed is the arithmetic mean of the speeds; the most probable speed is the speed at the peak of the Maxwell distribution. c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), c_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), c_mp = sqrt(2RT/M). Ratio: c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73. For oxygen at 300 K: c_rms = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300/0.032) = 484 m/s. Then c_avg = 484 x (1.60/1.73) = 447 m/s and c_mp = 484 x (1.41/1.73) = 395 m/s.

questions.question: Explain the concept of degrees of freedom and the law of equipartition of energy. Use them to find the internal energy per mole of monatomic and diatomic gases.
questions.answer: A degree of freedom is an independent way in which a molecule can store energy (an independent coordinate of its motion). A monatomic molecule can only translate along x, y, z: 3 degrees of freedom. A diatomic molecule also rotates about two axes perpendicular to the bond: 3 + 2 = 5 degrees of freedom. The law of equipartition states that in thermal equilibrium each degree of freedom carries an average energy of (1/2) k_B T per molecule, i.e. (1/2) R T per mole. Hence internal energy per mole U = (f/2) R T. Monatomic (f = 3): U = (3/2) R T. Diatomic (f = 5): U = (5/2) R T. This directly gives their specific heats C_v = (3/2)R and (5/2)R respectively.
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom + equipartition -> internal energy.

questions.question: Derive C_p - C_v = R for an ideal gas and hence obtain gamma for monatomic and diatomic gases.
questions.answer: For one mole of an ideal gas the internal energy is U = (f/2) R T, so the molar specific heat at constant volume is C_v = dU/dT = (f/2) R. When one mole is heated by dT at constant pressure, the first law gives heat = dU + work done. The work done in expansion at constant pressure is P dV; from PV = RT at constant P we get P dV = R dT. So heat at constant pressure per kelvin, C_p = dU/dT + R = C_v + R, i.e. C_p - C_v = R (Mayer's relation). The ratio gamma = C_p/C_v = (C_v + R)/C_v = 1 + R/C_v = 1 + 2/f. For a monatomic gas f = 3: gamma = 1 + 2/3 = 5/3 = 1.67. For a diatomic gas f = 5: gamma = 1 + 2/5 = 7/5 = 1.40.

questions.question: State the postulates of the kinetic theory of gases and explain how each idealises the behaviour of a real gas.
questions.answer: (1) A gas has a very large number of identical molecules in random motion - real gases indeed contain about 10^23 molecules per mole moving randomly, allowing statistical averages. (2) Molecular size and volume are negligible compared with the container and intermolecular spacing - true at low pressure where molecules are far apart, but not at high pressure where their own volume matters. (3) Molecules exert no force except during collisions and move in straight lines between them - valid when intermolecular attractions are weak, i.e. at high temperature/low density. (4) Collisions are perfectly elastic, conserving kinetic energy and momentum - this keeps the gas at steady temperature and pressure. (5) The collision time is negligible compared with the free-flight time. (6) Molecules obey Newton's laws and all directions are equally likely. These idealisations make the mathematics tractable and lead to PV = nRT; departures from them explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the mean free path of a gas molecule. Derive/quote its dependence on molecular size and density, and discuss how pressure and temperature affect it.
questions.answer: The mean free path lambda is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. A molecule of diameter d sweeps out a collision cylinder of cross-section pi d^2 as it moves; it collides with any molecule whose centre lies within this cylinder. Accounting for the relative motion of the target molecules introduces a factor sqrt(2), giving lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), where n = N/V is the number density. Thus lambda is larger for smaller molecules (proportional to 1/d^2) and for lower number density (proportional to 1/n). Using PV = N k_B T, n = P/(k_B T), so lambda = k_B T/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 P): the mean free path increases with temperature at constant pressure and decreases as pressure rises at constant temperature. At atmospheric pressure lambda is about 10^-7 m; in a good vacuum it can exceed the size of the container.
questions.explanation: Mean free path concept, formula and P, T dependence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A cylinder contains 2.0 moles of an ideal gas at 300 K. The universal gas constant is R = 8.314 J/mol/K and the volume of the cylinder is 0.0498 m^3.

(i) Write the ideal gas equation.
(ii) Calculate the pressure of the gas.
(iii) If the gas is heated at constant volume to 600 K, what is the new pressure?
(iv) State the gas law used in part (iii).
questions.answer: (i) PV = nRT. (ii) P = nRT/V = (2.0 x 8.314 x 300)/0.0498 = 4988/0.0498 = 1.00 x 10^5 Pa (approximately). (iii) At constant volume P is proportional to T, so doubling T from 300 K to 600 K doubles the pressure to 2.00 x 10^5 Pa. (iv) Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law: P/T = constant at constant volume.
questions.explanation: Ideal gas equation plus Gay-Lussac's law.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The kinetic theory gives the pressure of an ideal gas as P = (1/3)(Nm/V) c_rms^2 = (1/3) rho c_rms^2, where c_rms is the root-mean-square speed of the molecules.

(i) What causes gas pressure at the molecular level?
(ii) A gas of density 1.5 kg/m^3 exerts a pressure of 1.25 x 10^5 Pa. Find c_rms.
(iii) If the density is doubled while c_rms is unchanged, what happens to the pressure?
(iv) If c_rms doubles at fixed density, what happens to the pressure?
questions.answer: (i) Pressure is caused by the countless collisions of molecules with the container walls; each elastic impact reverses the molecule's momentum and delivers an impulse to the wall. (ii) c_rms = sqrt(3P/rho) = sqrt(3 x 1.25 x 10^5 / 1.5) = sqrt(2.5 x 10^5) = 500 m/s. (iii) P is proportional to rho, so doubling the density doubles the pressure to 2.5 x 10^5 Pa. (iv) P is proportional to c_rms^2, so doubling c_rms makes the pressure four times as large.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T, where k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. A container holds a mixture of helium and argon in thermal equilibrium at 300 K.

(i) Compare the average kinetic energies of the helium and argon atoms.
(ii) Calculate the average kinetic energy of an atom.
(iii) Which gas has the higher rms speed and why?
(iv) What happens to the average kinetic energy if the temperature is doubled?
questions.answer: (i) In thermal equilibrium both gases are at the same temperature, so their atoms have EQUAL average translational kinetic energies. (ii) KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300 = 6.21 x 10^-21 J. (iii) Helium has the higher rms speed. Since c_rms = sqrt(3 k_B T/m) and helium (mass 4 u) is lighter than argon (mass 40 u), the lighter helium atoms move faster at the same temperature. (iv) Doubling the temperature doubles the average kinetic energy, because KE_avg is proportional to T.
questions.explanation: KE_avg equal at same T; lighter gas faster.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Molecular speeds in a gas are described by three characteristic values: the most probable speed c_mp = sqrt(2RT/M), the average speed c_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)) and the rms speed c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M).

(i) Write these speeds in increasing order.
(ii) State the numerical ratio c_mp : c_avg : c_rms.
(iii) Calculate c_rms for nitrogen (M = 28 x 10^-3 kg/mol) at 300 K.
(iv) How does c_rms change if the temperature is raised to 1200 K?
questions.answer: (i) c_mp < c_avg < c_rms. (ii) c_mp : c_avg : c_rms = sqrt(2) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(3) = 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73. (iii) c_rms = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300/0.028) = sqrt(7482.6/0.028) = sqrt(267 236) = 517 m/s. (iv) c_rms is proportional to sqrt(T). Raising T from 300 K to 1200 K (a factor of 4) multiplies c_rms by sqrt(4) = 2, giving about 1034 m/s.
questions.explanation: Order, ratio and numerical rms speed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The law of equipartition of energy assigns an average energy of (1/2) k_B T to each degree of freedom of a molecule. Monatomic gases have 3 degrees of freedom and diatomic gases have 5 at ordinary temperature.

(i) State the number of degrees of freedom of a monatomic and a diatomic molecule.
(ii) Write the internal energy per mole of each.
(iii) Where do the two extra degrees of freedom of a diatomic molecule come from?
(iv) Find the internal energy of 3 moles of a monatomic gas at 400 K. (R = 8.314 J/mol/K.)
questions.answer: (i) Monatomic: 3 (all translational). Diatomic: 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). (ii) Monatomic U = (3/2) R T per mole; diatomic U = (5/2) R T per mole. (iii) The two extra degrees of freedom come from rotation of the diatomic molecule about the two axes perpendicular to the line joining the atoms. (iv) U = n(3/2)RT = 3 x 1.5 x 8.314 x 400 = 3 x 4988 = 14 965 J (about 15.0 kJ).
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom and internal energy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

For an ideal gas the molar specific heats obey C_v = (f/2)R and C_p = C_v + R, and gamma = C_p/C_v. Here f is the number of degrees of freedom and R = 8.314 J/mol/K.

(i) Find C_v, C_p and gamma for a monatomic gas.
(ii) Find C_v, C_p and gamma for a diatomic gas.
(iii) State Mayer's relation.
(iv) A gas is measured to have gamma = 1.4. What type of gas is it?
questions.answer: (i) Monatomic (f = 3): C_v = (3/2)R = 12.5 J/mol/K, C_p = C_v + R = 20.8 J/mol/K, gamma = 5/3 = 1.67. (ii) Diatomic (f = 5): C_v = (5/2)R = 20.8 J/mol/K, C_p = (7/2)R = 29.1 J/mol/K, gamma = 7/5 = 1.40. (iii) Mayer's relation: C_p - C_v = R. (iv) gamma = 1.4 = 7/5, so it is a diatomic gas.
questions.explanation: Specific heats and identification by gamma.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The mean free path of a gas molecule is lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), where d is the molecular diameter and n the number of molecules per unit volume. At atmospheric pressure lambda is about 10^-7 m.

(i) Define mean free path.
(ii) How does lambda change if the gas pressure is reduced at constant temperature?
(iii) How does lambda depend on the molecular diameter?
(iv) Why do gases diffuse slowly despite high molecular speeds?
questions.answer: (i) The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. (ii) Reducing the pressure at constant temperature reduces the number density n (since n = P/(k_B T)), so lambda increases (lambda proportional to 1/n). (iii) lambda is inversely proportional to d^2, so larger molecules have a shorter mean free path. (iv) Although molecular speeds are several hundred m/s, molecules collide extremely often (mean free path only about 10^-7 m) and change direction randomly at each collision, following a long zig-zag path. The net displacement therefore grows slowly, making diffusion slow.
questions.explanation: Mean free path properties and diffusion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The kinetic theory of gases rests on a set of postulates that idealise real gas molecules as tiny particles in random elastic motion.

(i) State any two postulates of the kinetic theory.
(ii) Which postulate explains why a gas exerts pressure on the walls?
(iii) Which two assumptions fail for a real gas at high pressure and low temperature?
(iv) Why must the number of molecules be very large?
questions.answer: (i) Two postulates: (a) a gas has a very large number of identical molecules in random motion in all directions; (b) collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic. (ii) The assumption that molecules move freely and collide elastically with the walls explains pressure - each rebounding molecule gives the wall an impulse, and the many impacts produce a steady pressure. (iii) At high pressure the molecular volume is no longer negligible, and at low temperature the intermolecular attractive forces are no longer negligible. (iv) A very large number of molecules is needed so that statistical averages (like <v^2> and pressure) are steady and well-defined rather than fluctuating.
questions.explanation: Postulates and their role and limits.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Boyle's law, Charles' law and Gay-Lussac's law describe how P, V and T of a fixed mass of gas are related, and combine into PV = nRT.

(i) A gas at 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and 300 K is compressed isothermally to half its volume. Find the new pressure.
(ii) State the law used.
(iii) The same gas is then heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 450 K. By what factor does the volume change?
(iv) State the law used in (iii).
questions.answer: (i) Isothermal compression: P1 V1 = P2 V2, so halving V doubles P. New pressure = 2.0 x 10^5 Pa. (ii) Boyle's law (constant temperature). (iii) At constant pressure V is proportional to T, so V changes by the factor 450/300 = 1.5 (volume increases by 50%). (iv) Charles' law (constant pressure).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The kinetic pressure relation PV = (1/3) N m c_rms^2 can be combined with the ideal gas law PV = N k_B T to interpret temperature.

(i) Show that KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T.
(ii) What does this tell us about the physical meaning of temperature?
(iii) Does the average kinetic energy depend on the mass of the molecule?
(iv) What is the average kinetic energy at absolute zero?
questions.answer: (i) Write PV = (1/3) N m c_rms^2 = (2/3) N (1/2 m c_rms^2) = (2/3) N (KE_avg). Setting this equal to PV = N k_B T gives (2/3) KE_avg = k_B T, so KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T. (ii) It means absolute temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules. (iii) No - KE_avg = (3/2) k_B T depends only on temperature, not on molecular mass; lighter molecules just move faster to have the same energy. (iv) At absolute zero (T = 0) the average translational kinetic energy is zero.
questions.explanation: Derives KE_avg = (3/2)k_B T and its meaning.
